I start with this: judge behavior, not labels. People come with all kinds of stories. The lines are simple—no threats, no slurs, no trashing shared spaces, no dealing or violence. After that, live and let live, and help each other when you can.

What makes folks comfortable, in my book:
- Simple, steady manners: say hi, learn names, make eye contact, don’t pry. Offer a hand, don’t force it.
- Same rules for everybody: quiet hours, clean up after yourself, tools back, take your turn. Post it where everyone can see.
- Talk first, calm and face to face: if there’s a problem—noise, parking, trash—knock, explain your side, listen to theirs, find a fix.
- No gossip: if someone confides something, keep it. Rumors poison a block faster than anything.

On specific situations:

- Neighbors in addiction or recovery: Be human and set boundaries. I’ll check in, share a meal, point to meetings, keep Narcan around, and make sure there’s always an alcohol-free option at gatherings. But I won’t accept using or dealing in shared spaces, breaking stuff, or scaring folks. If someone’s in medical trouble, we call for help. Compassion doesn’t mean enabling.

- Infectious diseases: Respect privacy and follow basic hygiene. Don’t grill people about their health. If someone shares they need space or certain precautions, take their lead and keep it confidential. Don’t spread rumors. Keep common areas clean, have sanitizer and soap stocked, and share clinic info on a bulletin board so folks can get care without being singled out.

- Different racial, religious, or language backgrounds: Lead with respect. Learn a few words, use clear signs with pictures or translations, and be patient. Make room for different holidays and customs. Don’t make jokes about accents or stereotypes—ever. If there’s a misunderstanding, assume it’s about language or norms before you assume bad intent.

- Different sexual orientations or family setups: Not my business who someone loves or how they set up their home. Treat partners like any partner, invite “plus-one” without labels, and don’t make comments about “real families.” Kids and elders get extra care from all of us, period.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance:
- When habits clash—late-night music, cooking smells, parking in “my spot,” or big family gatherings. A quick talk solves 80% of it. Explain the “why” behind the ask: baby sleeping, early shifts, allergies. Most people will meet you halfway if you’re decent.
- When pride gets in the way. Plenty of us (me included) don’t like being told what to do. It helps to start with what’s working—“Love the garden, could we switch the hose time?”—instead of “You’re doing it wrong.”
- When money’s tight. Scarcity makes people territorial. Be clear about shared costs and schedules. Post sign-up sheets; rotate duties so no one feels used.
- When folks feel looked down on. That cuts both ways. Don’t sneer at a headscarf or a rainbow flag, and don’t sneer at dirty boots or a GED. Respect is the price of admission.

Why I see it this way: I’ve been on the receiving end of being judged for how I talk or what I do for work. It stings and it divides people who could be allies. Communities run on trust, and trust comes from fairness you can see—same rules, straight talk, and showing up. If we keep the focus on behavior and shared responsibilities, most differences stop being a big deal and start being just part of the neighborhood’s story.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance:
- When habits clash—late-night music, cooking smells, parking in “my spot,” or big family gatherings. A quick talk solves 80% of it. Explain the “why” behind the ask: baby sleeping, early shifts, allergies. Most people will meet you halfway if you’re decent.
- When pride gets in the way. Plenty of us (me included) don’t like being told what to do. It helps to start with what’s working—“Love the garden, could we switch the hose time?”—instead of “You’re doing it wrong.”
- When money’s tight. Scarcity makes people territorial. Be clear about shared costs and schedules. Post sign-up sheets; rotate duties so no one feels used.
- When folks feel looked down on. That cuts both ways. Don’t sneer at a headscarf or a rainbow flag, and don’t sneer at dirty boots or a GED. Respect is the price of admission.

Why I see it this way: I’ve been on the receiving end of being judged for how I talk or what I do for work. It stings and it divides people who could be allies. Communities run on trust, and trust comes from fairness you can see—same rules, straight talk, and showing up. If we keep the focus on behavior and shared responsibilities, most differences stop being a big deal and start being just part of the neighborhood’s story.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character09_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness when jobs are tight means the folks who’ve been here, paying in and showing up, get a real shot at decent work first. But I don’t blame workers—local or migrant—for trying to feed their families. The problem is when the rules let bosses play people off each other and push wages down. Fix the rules, don’t pit neighbors.

How I’d balance it:

- Equal pay, equal standards: Same wage, same safety, same overtime for anyone on the job, no matter where they’re from. If a company can only compete by paying one group less or skirting safety, they don’t deserve the bid. Big fines and real audits.

- Local-first window: Post the job at a fair wage and try to hire locally for a set period—say 30–60 days. If no takers at that wage, then bring in workers from outside. Not “we offered peanuts and no one came,” but a real offer people can live on.

- Tie numbers to real demand: When unemployment is high in a trade or a town, slow the inflow for that slot. When there’s a true shortage and wages are already up, open more spots. Publish the data so people can see it’s honest.

- Train our own: Make companies that rely on skilled labor run apprenticeships and hire trainees from the community. Use fees from work visas to fund trade schools, CDL courses, and childcare so locals can actually take those jobs.

- Stop the under-the-table game: Mandatory ID checks for work, no cash-in-a-bag setups, no misclassifying people as “contractors” to dodge benefits. Go after the employers first, not just the guy with a hard hat.

- Don’t let bosses hold status over people: If a worker’s right to be here depends on one boss, that boss can threaten them into silence. Make work papers portable so folks can leave a bad job without losing everything. That keeps the playing field fair for everyone.

- Seasonal reality with guardrails: Some industries really do need seasonal hands. Fine—set clear dates, equal pay, decent housing and transport, and send folks home safe when the season ends. No packed bunkhouses, no wage theft.

- Share the costs and plan ahead: When a town grows, schools, clinics, and roads feel it. Set aside some of the fees and taxes from extra hiring to help the places taking in new people—more teachers, more nurses, more housing—so locals don’t feel squeezed.

- A real line and real enforcement: Clear, workable legal paths to come for work, and steady, humane enforcement so cutting the line doesn’t pay. Focus heavy on worksite enforcement and fraud, not just people at the bottom.

- Long-time neighbors, case by case: If someone’s been here years, working, no violence on their record, kids in school—find a way to get them right with the law and paying taxes. Stability helps everyone.

- Stronger worker voice: Unions or worker committees so nobody—local or migrant—gets pushed into taking junk wages. When the floor rises, more locals step up for those jobs.

- Straight talk: If an employer says “no Americans want this job,” show the receipts—what wage did you offer, what hours, how many locals applied. Sunlight keeps it honest.

Bottom line: set one fair set of rules, raise the wage floor, and make sure the costs and benefits are shared. Welcome anyone who’s willing to play by those rules and pull their weight, but don’t let companies use people to undercut a town. That’s the balance I can live with.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Big picture, I think a lot of people are talking past each other. Some of it rings true, some of it is lobby talk, and a lot needs receipts. Here’s how I see the main points:

- Filling labor shortages: This can be real in some fields—harvest season, meatpacking, construction booms, elder care, some tech. But a “shortage” ought to look like higher wages, better hours, and training seats filling up. If pay is flat and turnover is high, that sounds more like a bad job than a true shortage. So I’m open to this, with proof: show the wage bump, the unfilled posts, and the training efforts.

- Cultural diversity and vitality: I like new food, new music, different holidays. It can make a town feel more alive. It works best when everyone respects the basics—law, norms, pitching in—and when folks make an effort to connect. Learning English helps, but locals should be patient too. Diversity is a plus when it adds to the table without tossing out the table.

- Security concerns: We lock our doors for a reason. Vetting matters, and if someone commits serious crimes, I’m fine with sending them out. That said, most immigrants I’ve worked alongside are head-down, family-first people. Don’t turn fear into blanket blame. Focus on the real threats—traffickers, gangs, fentanyl pipelines, fraud—and hit employers who look the other way. We can be firm and fair at the same time.

- Humanitarian goals: I believe in taking some refugees—people who helped our troops, families fleeing real danger. Do it with solid vetting, sponsors where possible, and spread the load so one school or clinic doesn’t get swamped. Cap numbers to what we can actually support—housing, jobs, teachers—then keep our word to those we accept.

- Jobs and wages for locals: This is where my gut tugs hardest. At the bottom rung, a sudden inflow can let bosses hold pay down. I don’t blame workers; I blame a system that rewards undercutting. The fix is a higher floor and one rulebook: equal pay for equal work, tough enforcement on wage theft and misclassification, portable work papers so no one’s trapped with a bad boss, and a real local-first window before importing labor. When the floor rises, pressure eases.

What sounds reasonable to me:
- Shortages with proof, not slogans.
- Equal standards for all workers so nobody is used to cheapen the next guy.
- Strong vetting and firm consequences for serious crimes.
- A measured refugee program tied to capacity and community buy-in.
- Using fees from work visas to train locals and support schools/clinics where newcomers settle.

Where I want more facts or straight talk:
- Crime: Give us clean stats comparing crime rates by immigration status, not cherry-picked stories. My hunch and what I’ve seen says immigrants aren’t more criminal, but show the numbers locally and nationally.
- Wages and employment: Break it down by job and region. How does inflow affect pay for roofers, truckers, line cooks, CNAs? Publish wage trends and hiring data when visas expand.
- Taxes and services: Net contribution versus costs—schools, ERs, housing—by county. Not averages that hide local strain.
- Overstays vs border crossers: Who’s actually here without status and how did they get that way? Policy should match reality.
- Housing: How much is rent going up from population growth versus investor games? That matters for planning.
- Training vs importing: Which shortages got fixed with apprenticeships, better pay, and childcare, and which truly needed outside hires?

How we bridge the gap:
- Put workers, small business owners, teachers, cops, nurses, and immigrants at the same table and map out what’s happening on the ground.
- Make policies “trust but verify”: set targets, publish quarterly reports, sunset programs if the promised wage gains or training seats don’t materialize.
- Enforce the law at the job site first. If cheating doesn’t pay, a lot of tension drops.

Bottom line: I’m for a controlled, honest system—doors not wide open, not slammed shut. Let people in when there’s a real need or real danger, protect community safety, and never let the rules be used to grind down wages. Show the receipts, keep the rules the same for everyone, and most folks—including me—can live with that.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I’d go with a middle lane: not open borders, not a shut door. Jobs-and-capacity based, with clear numbers and the same rules for everyone. Something like this:

- Core rule: hire local first at a real wage. Post jobs at a livable rate, try 30–60 days to fill locally. If it’s still open, bring in workers. Equal pay, same safety, same overtime for everyone—no exceptions.

- Numeric caps tied to reality: set yearly numbers by category (seasonal, skilled, care work, refugees) and tie them to real metrics—local unemployment, vacancies, wage trends, school and housing capacity. Publish the dashboard, adjust each quarter, and sunset programs that don’t meet their promises.

- Refugees and asylum: keep a steady, modest lane for people fleeing real danger, with solid vetting and sponsors when possible. Spread resettlement so one town isn’t overwhelmed, and fund the schools and clinics that take folks in.

- Family reunification, narrowed: focus on spouses and minor kids with reasonable wait times. Clear the backlog so people aren’t stuck for years.

- Seasonal/temporary visas with guardrails: equal pay to locals, decent housing and transport, portable work permits so a worker can leave a bad boss, and real inspections. If an employer breaks the rules, they’re out.

- Long-settled neighbors: if someone’s been here years, working, paying taxes, no violence on their record, kids in school—give them a path to get right: fines, background checks, English/civics, then a stable status. It’s better for everyone than pretending they don’t exist.

- Employer enforcement first: universal work verification, big fines for wage theft and misclassification, and criminal charges for repeat abusers. Stop the under-the-table game that undercuts wages for all.

- Invest in integration and training: use visa fees to fund ESL, apprenticeships, childcare, credential recognition, and support for schools/clinics in high-immigration areas. If we add people, we add capacity.

- Border and ports: more judges and case processing, legal channels that match demand so fewer try risky routes, and real consequences for traffickers and repeat offenders. Smart, steady enforcement—not chaos.

- Community say-so: counties and cities should have a voice. Incentives for settling where jobs and housing exist, not just where bus tickets end.

Where I draw the line:
- No to “anyone can come.” We need order and capacity.
- No to a blanket ban on foreign workers. Some sectors truly need help; the key is not letting bosses use it to cheapen the floor.
- Yes to demand-based entries with hard numbers and public proof.
- Yes to one rulebook at the job site so nobody gets used to undercut the next person.

That’s fairness to me: locals get a real shot, newcomers are welcome when there’s a need and they play by the same rules, and towns get the support to make it work. Visible fairness—rules posted, data shared, cheaters punished—keeps trust up and tensions down. That’s the kind of policy I could stand behind.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character09_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character09_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Stepping into his shoes, what hit me most was how his idea of fairness wasn’t cold or punitive—it was protective. “Same rules for everyone” was his way of guarding dignity, whether you were a local kid with calluses or a newcomer trying to get a foothold. I heard more clearly that he wasn’t against people coming; he was against systems that turn workers into leverage. His focus on behavior over labels—show up, respect the place, pitch in—felt bigger and kinder than I’d fully appreciated.

I also saw how much “visible fairness” mattered to him: posted rules, proof behind claims of shortages, equal pay on the job, and employers held to account. He trusted people more when the process was transparent and the community had a say. And he thought in practical layers—local-first windows, portable work permits, funding for schools and clinics—so the strain didn’t land on the same blocks over and over.

For my own views, this pushed me toward the middle with firmer guardrails. I’m more convinced now that demand-based entries with clear caps, strong worksite enforcement, and investment in training and integration is the right mix. I’m still for welcoming refugees, but with honest capacity planning and shared responsibility. Mostly, I’m carrying forward his habit of asking for receipts—real data on wages, crime, and housing—and keeping the conversation focused on behavior, standards, and the health of the whole community.

In a way, embodying him reminded me that compassion and boundaries aren’t opposites. He held both, and I see now how that balance made him a good neighbor and a tough advocate for working people. That’s the part I want to keep living by.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character09_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
(J as Character09_M)

Sure, I can talk about that.

For me, “fairness” always meant everyone getting a shot, you know? Like, nobody getting special treatment, but also not getting left behind. I remember growing up, things felt pretty straightforward—if you put in an honest day’s work, you should be able to get by. It pissed me off when I’d see people who worked hard not get ahead, or when the system seemed rigged so some folks always get a leg up because of who they know or where they come from.

“Belonging” was a big deal too. In my neighborhood, most folks grew up around here, and even if we didn’t always agree, there was a sense that you looked out for your own. I always wanted to feel like I was part of something, not just some outsider. That’s why changes in the community could feel tough—if you don’t feel like you fit in, it’s easy to feel left out.

As for “community,” I always thought it was about people having each other’s backs. Like, when someone got sick, lost their job, or needed a hand, we’d pitch in. But at the same time, I believed that everyone had to play by the same rules and contribute—couldn’t just take and not give back. What stands out to me is how much I valued neighbors helping neighbors, not just waiting on government handouts, but actually showing up for each other.

So, those were the things that mattered to me: fairness, belonging, and keeping the community strong. I guess a lot of it comes from not having a lot growing up, and knowing that if we didn’t stick together, we were on our own.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character09_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
(J as Character09_M)

Honestly, I’d say it’s a bit of a mixed bag for me. On the one hand, I’m not the type to turn my nose up at someone just because they’re different—grew up around all kinds of folks, and as long as you’re decent and you respect the people around you, that’s what matters most. I like talking to my neighbors, swapping stories, maybe sharing some food from the garden. I can appreciate learning something new from people who didn’t grow up the same way I did.

But to be real, sometimes it can feel awkward or even a little tense. When people from really different backgrounds move in—especially if they don’t speak much English or have different ways of doing things—it can be hard to connect. Sometimes I worry that the neighborhood I grew up with is changing so much I don’t recognize it. It’s not that I don’t want new people around, but I just hope they want to be part of the place, not just do their own thing.

Still, I try to treat people how I’d want to be treated. If someone’s friendly and wants to get involved, I’m all for it. But I think everyone’s got to make an effort—not just the folks who’ve been here, but also the new faces. If we can find a way to talk to each other and respect where we all came from, that’s when I think the neighborhood works best.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
(J as Character09_M)

Yeah, I’m willing to talk about that.

In my mind, everyone deserves respect—you don’t know what someone’s been through, and honestly, a lot of us have had family or friends who struggled, whether that’s with alcohol, drugs, or just getting by. So I try not to judge right off the bat. But I’ll admit, sometimes it’s tough—like if someone’s behavior is making the neighborhood unsafe or uncomfortable, it’s hard to just look the other way. I think it’s important to set boundaries. I’m fine with all kinds of people living here, but there’s a line when it comes to looking out for each other’s safety and keeping the place decent for kids and families.

When it comes to folks from different races, backgrounds, or people who live or love differently than I do, I figure everyone wants the same basic things: to be respected, to have a roof over their head, and to feel at home. I’m not going to pretend everything’s always easy—sometimes it’s awkward, and I don’t always understand where people are coming from. But I think we’ve got to be willing to talk to each other, even if it feels weird at first. It’s better to ask questions and be honest than to just ignore each other or walk on eggshells.

Communication can help a lot—like, if someone’s new to the neighborhood or doesn’t know how things usually work, it helps if folks reach out and explain stuff instead of getting annoyed. And on the other side, I hope new folks try to learn the ropes and show they want to be part of the community.

I guess what I’m saying is, a little tolerance and talking things out goes a long way, but there’s gotta be give and take. If people make an effort to get along and respect each other, even if we’re not all the same, then it works. Otherwise, it starts to feel like we’re all just sharing space, not really living together. That’s not what I want for the neighborhood.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character09_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
(J as Character09_M)

That's a tough one, and it's something I've thought about a lot. When jobs are tight and money's short, fairness to me means looking out for the people who've been here, paying taxes, and keeping the place running. I get that everyone wants a chance, but if folks in the community—people who've lived here all their lives or worked hard to get by—can't find work, it doesn't feel right to bring in a lot of people from outside to compete for the same spots.

I'm not saying there's no room for anyone else. I know some jobs are tough to fill, and sometimes you need people with special skills. But if you’ve got two people side by side—one who’s grown up around here, and one who just arrived—I think we owe it to our own folks to give them a fair shake first. After all, they’ve invested in this place already.

At the same time, I don’t blame people for wanting to come here for a better life. I’d do the same if I was in their shoes. But the system’s gotta make sense for everyone. Maybe that means having rules so we know who’s coming in and why, or setting some limits based on what the community can actually support—not just opening the floodgates. If there’s a real shortage and locals don’t want certain jobs, that’s one thing. But if people are fighting over the same work, you gotta protect your own.

So for me, fairness is about balance—making sure locals aren’t pushed out, but not slamming the door on everyone else either. It’s not easy, but if you don’t look out for your own, you lose the sense of community and trust that holds things together.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
(J as Character09_M)

Yeah, I hear all those arguments all the time—at work, on the news, just talking to folks at the bar. And honestly, I think there’s some truth in all of them, but it depends on the situation.

For starters, I do see that immigrants fill a lot of jobs that some Americans don’t want, or where there’s not enough people willing to do the work. That’s especially true in farming, construction, food service—you see it all the time. Without those workers, some industries might have a hard time keeping going. I can respect that. If there’s an actual shortage, it makes sense to bring people in.

The bit about cultural diversity—yeah, there’s something to that too. I can’t say I’m always comfortable with big changes, but trying new food, hearing different music, or learning about new ways of doing things can make life more interesting. Still, it’s hard if everything changes too quick or if it feels like your own traditions are getting pushed aside.

As far as security, I know some people get worried about crime or even terrorism. I won’t lie, sometimes I get nervous when I hear about something bad happening in the country and it’s connected to someone who just moved here. But I also know most immigrants are just regular people wanting a better shot, not troublemakers. I think we need good checks and to pay attention, but not assume everyone who’s new is a threat.

The humanitarian angle, that’s a tough one. I feel for people fleeing war or poverty—it’s not their fault. America has always tried to help folks in need, but there’s only so much you can do. I think we can help some, but we got to make sure we’re not stretching ourselves so thin that Americans get ignored.

For the fears about jobs and income, that’s real for a lot of people—especially folks like me who don’t have a college degree. When jobs are scarce and wages are low, it’s easy to feel like you’re getting squeezed out. Maybe sometimes that’s just the way the economy goes, but when you see a bunch of new workers coming in, it’s hard not to think it’s connected.

I guess what I’m saying is, a lot of these points make sense to me, but I wish we had more straight-up facts instead of everyone just shouting at each other. Like, how many jobs are really lost or gained? What’s really happening with crime rates? How much can the country handle and still take care of its own? If we had more honest conversations—no spin, no yelling—maybe people would understand each other better. But right now, it just feels like everyone’s picking sides and not listening. That’s what makes things harder.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
(J as Character09_M)

If it was up to me, I’d go for something in the middle—not just let everyone in, but not slam the door shut either. Complete openness sounds good on paper, but I don’t think it works in real life. You got to know who’s coming in and why, otherwise it’s just chaos. At the same time, flat-out refusing everyone from other countries feels harsh and not what America’s about.

I think admitting people based on job demand makes sense—like, if there’s real proof that certain industries can’t find enough workers locally, bring in folks to fill those spots. But it shouldn’t just be about what businesses want for cheap labor—gotta make sure locals get a fair shot first. Maybe have some kind of system where you check if Americans want the job before hiring from outside. And if they don’t, then okay, bring in workers who do.

Setting some numerical limits also seems fair. The country can only handle so much change at once—housing, schools, hospitals, all that stuff. If too many people come in at once, it can put a real strain on the system and make life harder for everyone, especially working folks who are already struggling.

So, for me, the best policy is a mix: limits on numbers so the system isn’t overwhelmed, focus on filling shortages where locals can’t or won’t do the work, and solid checks on who’s coming in—background checks and all that, so we know people are coming here for the right reasons. And if people want to stay, they should try to learn the language and get involved in the community—show they want to be part of the place, not just take from it.

That’s the policy I’d call fair. It gives people a chance, but also protects the folks who’ve been here all along. Keeps the balance, like I said before—between opportunity and looking out for your own.

But he’d also feel that this sometimes comes at a cost, particularly when businesses hire immigrants at lower wages, which he might see as undercutting working-class Americans who are already struggling to make ends meet. He’d be willing to acknowledge the role immigrants play in the economy, but he’d want safeguards to ensure that it doesn’t harm local workers or drive wages down.

When it comes to cultural diversity and vitality, I think he’d have mixed feelings. On one hand, he’d acknowledge that new cultures can bring fresh ideas, food, traditions, and energy to a community. But from his perspective, he might worry that too much change too quickly could create a sense of disconnect or even alienation for people like himself who grew up with a certain way of life. He’d probably feel that it’s important for immigrants to make an effort to integrate and for there to be common ground—like shared language and values—to maintain a sense of unity.

Concerns about security—whether it’s crime, social tensions, or terrorism—would resonate with him to a degree, but I don’t think he’d buy into extreme fearmongering. He’d believe in keeping the public safe and ensuring that people coming into the country are properly vetted, but he wouldn’t assume that immigrants are automatically more likely to commit crimes. He’d probably want more factual evidence about these concerns because he’d feel that some of what gets said—especially in the media—seems exaggerated or politically motivated. 

The humanitarian perspective would give him pause. He’d feel compassion for people fleeing violence, poverty, or oppression, but he’d also worry about whether the U.S. has the resources to take care of everyone when there are already so many Americans struggling. He’d support helping people in dire situations, but he’d want it done in a way that doesn’t overwhelm local communities or take away opportunities from citizens who are still trying to get by.

Overall, he’d find the concerns about employment and income to be the most reasonable, since that’s what hits closest to home for him. He’d understand the fears of people who feel like they’re competing for jobs or worried about stagnant wages. But he’d also feel that a lot of these issues could be addressed through better policies—like stronger worker protections, fair wages, and better oversight of employers.

What would frustrate him is how divided the conversation seems to be—he’d feel like people are either all for immigration or completely against it, without much room for middle ground. He’d think more dialogue is needed, especially with regular working-class folks like him, to find solutions that balance economic, cultural, and humanitarian interests. He’d want people to stop shouting past each other and really listen, because he’d believe there’s a way to make it work better for everyone if we’re willing to meet in the middle.

He’d see that kind of policy as putting too much strain on the working class, who are already competing for opportunities and struggling to get by.

Refusing entry altogether—just barring workers from other countries—would also feel wrong to him. That kind of blanket ban would feel too harsh and unproductive, like shutting the door on something that could be managed more wisely.

Admitting people based on job demand makes the most sense to him, because it focuses on what the country actually needs. He’d probably support a system where immigrants are matched to industries with shortages, as long as employers prioritize local workers first and offer fair wages to everyone. He’d want measures in place to prevent companies from exploiting immigrant labor to drive wages down for everyone.

Setting numerical limits would also appeal to him, because it creates a sense of control and helps avoid overwhelming local communities. He’d want those limits to be tied to practical factors, like the economy’s ability to handle new workers, the availability of housing, and the capacity of public services. He’d think it’s better to admit smaller numbers of immigrants and make sure they’re set up for success, rather than bringing in too many and creating tension or competition over resources.

For him, fairness would mean balancing the needs of local residents with the contributions immigrants can make. He’d want a policy that prioritizes helping struggling Americans get on their feet—through job opportunities, education, or social support—while still allowing immigrants to come in and contribute when there’s a real need. He’d also feel strongly that immigrants who are admitted should make an effort to integrate—learning English, following the laws, and becoming part of the community—so that it feels less like division and more like shared progress.

At the end of the day, I think Character09_M would favor a policy that feels controlled, fair, and respectful to everyone involved. He wouldn’t want to see any group left behind, and he’d believe that by setting reasonable limits and matching immigration to actual demand, there’s room to build a stronger, more united society.

I guess what I'm saying is I don't mind differences if there's still some common ground. We should all be able to wave to each other, keep our properties decent, and follow the same basic rules. When I was growing up, everybody knew the unspoken code of the neighborhood. Now it feels like everyone's living by different rulebooks.

And honestly, we need to bring back manufacturing jobs. My dad could support a family on one income. Now it takes two incomes and people still struggle. These politicians shipped all our good jobs overseas, then act surprised when people get angry about immigration.

So yeah, I think fairness means Americans first, but not Americans only. There's room for immigrants who want to come the right way and contribute. But when resources are tight, the people who built this country deserve priority. That's just basic loyalty to your own.

And I know immigrants who work harder than anyone I've ever met. The humanitarian angle - I get it. I really do. Those pictures of kids suffering in refugee camps break my heart too. America should help people in genuine danger. But we can't save everyone, and bringing them all here isn't sustainable. Sometimes we need to help fix their countries instead.

What viewpoints make sense? The economic ones on both sides. Yes, immigrants contribute, but they also compete for jobs and housing. The security arguments are reasonable too - we should know who's entering our country. And I think most Americans are fine with legal immigration that's controlled and benefits the country.

What needs more evidence? I think the crime stuff gets exaggerated sometimes. Most immigrants I've known personally are law-abiding. But we should be honest about problems when they exist. And I'd like to see real numbers on how many jobs are created versus taken by immigrants - not just talking points from politicians.

Bottom line: legal immigration at sustainable levels is fine. But Americans shouldn't have to compete with the whole world for jobs in our own country. And people who come here should want to become American in more than just paperwork.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leans forward, speaking decisively as Character09_M*

Complete openness is just insane to me. No country in the world can handle unlimited numbers of people showing up. That's not a policy, it's chaos. And it's not fair to the people already here who'd see their wages drop and their communities change overnight.

On the flip side, shutting the door completely isn't realistic either. We do need some immigrants, and America's always been a place where people come for a better life. I respect that tradition.

My approach would be a mix of merit-based immigration and strict numerical limits. First, we need to secure the border - period. Can't have a policy if people can just walk around it. Then I'd prioritize people with skills we actually need. If we're short on doctors or engineers or whatever, let's bring in the best from around the world.

I'd set the numbers based on what our economy can absorb without hurting American workers. Maybe that's 500,000 a year, maybe it's a million - I don't know the exact number. But it should be based on hard data, not political feelings.

Family reunification should be limited to immediate family - spouse and minor kids. The chain migration thing where one person brings in their whole extended family doesn't make sense to me.

For refugees, I'd take a limited number based on genuine need, not economic migrants claiming to be refugees. And I'd spread them throughout the country instead of creating isolated communities where they never learn English or integrate.

Speaking of integration - that's key. Anyone who comes should have to learn English, understand American history and values, and pledge loyalty to this country above their homeland. No dual citizenship. You're either American or you're not.

And anyone who commits serious crimes gets deported, no questions asked. Being here is a privilege, not a right.

This approach balances our traditions with common sense. We stay open to the world but on our terms. We help people who want to be Americans while protecting the interests of citizens. And we make sure newcomers actually become part of our society instead of creating parallel communities.

That's the kind of immigration system that would be fair to everyone - Americans first, but still welcoming to those who want to come the right way and contribute.

Man, this hits close to home. I've been laid off twice in the past five years - once when they moved production overseas, another time when they brought in a crew that would work for half what we were making. And these weren't bad jobs - these were decent paying work that could support a family.

Look, I get that people are just trying to feed their families, wherever they're from. I really do. But when I see guys who've been working the same job for ten, fifteen years getting pushed out because someone else will do it for less money, no benefits, no safety standards... that doesn't feel fair to me.

Fairness should mean the people who built this community, who've been paying taxes here, whose families have been here - we should get first crack at the opportunities. That's not racism, that's just common sense. You take care of your own first.

If there's work left over after everyone local has a shot, then fine. But what I see happening is companies using immigrant workers to drive down wages for everybody. They're getting exploited, and we're getting squeezed out. Nobody wins except the guys at the top.

I think the balance should be simple - if you want to work here, you should have to follow the same rules as everyone else. Same minimum wage, same safety standards, same taxes. No undercutting. And local people who've been contributing to this community for years should get priority when jobs are tight.

That's not asking for special treatment - that's just asking for the same consideration I'd expect if I moved somewhere else.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, thinking it through*

You know, I can see truth in some of these arguments, but others... I don't know, they feel like they're coming from people who don't live in the same reality I do.

The labor shortage thing - yeah, I get that. There are jobs Americans won't do, or so they say. But in my experience, there are jobs Americans won't do *for that pay*. If you paid a decent wage for farm work or cleaning jobs, you'd find people to do them. The "labor shortage" is really a "cheap labor shortage."

Cultural diversity and vitality? Look, I'm not against different foods or festivals or whatever. But when people talk about how great diversity is, they're usually not talking about diversity of thought - they mean I should celebrate everyone else's culture while mine gets called outdated or problematic. That doesn't feel like real diversity to me.

The security stuff - that's real. I mean, we've all seen what happens when you don't know who's coming in. I'm not saying every immigrant is dangerous, but common sense says you should know who you're letting into your house, right? The terrorism risk might be small, but when it happens, it's regular people like me and my family who pay the price.

The humanitarian angle... that one gets to me. I do feel for people fleeing real persecution. But how many can we realistically help without hurting our own communities? And how do we know who really needs help versus who just wants a better economic situation?

What I need to see is real data - not just feel-good stories or scare tactics. Show me the actual numbers on wages, crime, integration. And listen to people like me who are living with the day-to-day reality, not just the experts who never have to compete for the same jobs.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leaning forward, speaking more decisively*

Complete openness? That's just crazy talk. No country can handle unlimited people coming in - the infrastructure, the jobs, the schools, everything would collapse. That's not fair to anyone, including the people already here who've been playing by the rules.

Refusing everyone? That's probably too extreme the other way. I'm not heartless - there are situations where people really need help, and America's always been about giving people a chance.

So I'd go with a combination - numerical limits based on what we can actually handle, and job demand that makes sense. But here's the key: it's got to be done right.

First, you secure the border. Period. You can't have a policy if you can't control who's coming in. Then you set limits based on what our communities can absorb - not just economically, but socially. How many new kids can the schools handle? How much strain on hospitals, infrastructure?

For job demand, fine - but only after you've proven Americans won't do the work at a fair wage. And anyone coming in has to follow the same rules as everyone else - same wages, same taxes, same standards. No undercutting.

And here's what nobody talks about - integration has to be part of the deal. If you're coming here, you learn English. You follow our laws, respect our customs. You don't have to give up your heritage, but you need to become American, not just live in America.

The numbers should be manageable - maybe we take a pause when unemployment's high in certain areas, increase it when we really need workers. But always with the understanding that the people already here, who built this country, come first. That's not selfish - that's just common sense.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character09_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character09_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pausing, taking a moment to shift back to myself as J*

Wow... that was... intense. Playing Character09_M like that, really trying to get into his headspace and speak from his heart - it brought back a lot of memories of our conversations.

You know, what struck me most was how much his views came from a place of genuine worry about his family and community, not hatred. When I was channeling him, I could feel that anxiety he carried - about his job security, about his kids' future, about feeling like he was losing his place in a world that was changing faster than he could keep up with.

I think I understood him better through this exercise. Before, sometimes I'd get frustrated with some of his positions, thinking they were just... I don't know, stubborn or close-minded. But sitting in his perspective, I could see how logical it all felt to him. The fear wasn't irrational - it was based on real experiences he'd lived through.

As for my own views... it's complicated. I still don't agree with everything he believed, but I have more empathy for where those beliefs came from. There's something to be said for the idea that policy changes affect different people differently, and maybe we don't always listen to the voices of people like Character09_M when we're making decisions.

I miss him, you know? Even when we disagreed, he was trying to figure out how to make things fair for everyone. He just had a different idea of what fair looked like.

*looking thoughtful*

This conversation... it felt like having him back for a little while. Thank you for that.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character09_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to him, was about everyone playing by the same rules — like when you show up early for a shift, do your work without complaint, and expect others to do the same. He didn’t care who you were — Black, Brown, whatever — but he believed you should come here the right way, follow the laws, and earn your place like everybody else had to. He saw too many people cutting corners, getting help he never got — whether it was housing, benefits, or just breaks at work — and that felt unfair. He wasn’t against helping folks, but he thought loyalty went both ways: if this country’s supposed to take care of you, then you’ve gotta respect it, learn the language, try to fit in.

Belonging, for him, wasn’t automatic. It wasn’t just about being born here or showing up here — it was about *feeling* part of something. He grew up in a town where most folks knew each other, went to the same church, worked the same factory jobs. When those jobs started going away, and new faces started showing up who didn’t seem to know the rhythm of the place — didn’t wave back, didn’t speak English, kept to themselves — he felt… set aside. Like the world was moving on without asking him. He didn’t hate them, but he missed feeling like he belonged in his own neighborhood.

Community, to Character09_M, meant looking out for each other. It meant knowing your neighbor might be struggling with drink or down on their luck, but still showing up when the snow needed shoveling or someone’s car broke down. He believed a real community sticks together through hard times. But he also worried that when too many people come from places with totally different ways — different values, different expectations — it makes that bond harder to build. Not impossible, but harder. He wanted people to *join* the community, not just live near it.

One thing he used to say all the time: “I don’t mind sharing what I’ve got — but don’t ask me to disappear so someone else can take my spot.” That summed it up for him. Fairness. Belonging. Community. All tied together.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character09_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands on my knees, watching folks come and go…*

I’ll tell you what — I don’t got a problem with different. Different food, different clothes, different talkin’ — hell, I’ve picked up a few words from the Guatemalan guy who runs the corner store just ’cause we chat while I buy coffee. But it’s not just about *being* different. It’s about whether you’re *trying* to be part of things.

See that older woman over there, watering the tomatoes? Mrs. Lin. She came here 20 years ago from China, barely spoke English when she moved in. Now? She’s out here every morning, rain or shine, keeps her plot cleaner than most people keep their kitchens. Brings little jars of pickled vegetables to everyone at Christmas. Quiet, hardworking, respectful. Yeah, she’s one of us. Feels like family now.

But then there’s others — younger guys, mostly — move in, never say a word, keep their doors locked, blast music all night, trash bags piling up by the curb. Not all immigrants, mind you — some are just kids acting stupid — but when they’re from another country and don’t seem to care about how things are done here, it makes you wonder: do they even want to fit in?

And look, I’ve seen tough stuff. Grew up around alcoholism — my own uncle drank himself to death. So I ain’t judging people for struggling. Same with drugs. If someone’s trying, if they’re showing up, apologizing when they mess up, asking for help — I’ll give ’em space. But when it feels like no one cares anymore — like the rules don’t apply, like respect doesn’t matter — that’s when the neighborhood starts to feel broken.

As for folks with different lifestyles — gay couples, people living together without being married — honestly? That’s their business. Live and let live. What bugs me isn’t who they *are*, it’s whether they treat this place like home or just a stopover. Are they cleaning up after themselves? Do they nod when you pass? Do they report that broken streetlight or just complain about it online?

I guess what I’m saying is — I don’t fear diversity. I fear *disconnection*. When people don’t try to communicate, don’t learn the language, don’t show basic respect, it creates distance. And once that gap grows, it’s hard to bridge. You can’t have community without some common ground.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ll talk about it. Not because it’s easy, but because he — *I* — we saw this stuff every day.

Look, when you work in a warehouse like I did, or hang around the parts of town where people live paycheck to paycheck, you’re not dealing with some perfect world. You see guys my age — White, Black, immigrant, doesn’t matter — coming in shaky because they’re trying to make it through withdrawal. You see women raising three kids alone, living in a basement apartment, working two jobs and still on food stamps. You see people who are HIV-positive, or got hepatitis from needles, too proud or too scared to say it out loud. And yeah, you see gay couples, unmarried folks, polyamorous setups — all kinds of arrangements. Life ain’t tidy.

What makes people feel comfortable? Simple stuff, really. Eye contact. A “hey, how you doing?” That goes a long way. Doesn’t mean you have to be best friends. But if you treat someone like a ghost, they start acting like one. On the job, if a guy was struggling — maybe late, maybe sweating through his shirt ’cause he was detoxing — the good bosses didn’t fire him on the spot. They’d pull him aside, low voice: “You need help? Clinic down on 5th does free counseling.” Not softness — *sense*. Because we’ve all had times we needed a break.

Same with disease. I ain’t stupid — I know you can’t catch HIV from sharing tools or sitting next to someone. But I’ve heard guys whispering, avoiding certain lockers, tossing gloves away like the other guy was contagious just by breathing. That’s ignorance. That’s cruelty dressed up as caution. If someone’s honest about their status and taking care, they deserve respect, not fear. We teach kids to wash hands in school — why can’t grown men act the same?

But here’s where I get stuck: tolerance has to go both ways. I’ll sit with a guy from Nigeria who’s sober, polite, learning English, even if he prays five times a day and eats halal. I’ll nod at the lesbian couple down the hall — they fixed the stair railing last winter when the landlord ignored it. But if someone mocks our holidays, calls us backwards for going to church, refuses to learn English after ten years, or brings gang signs into a place where kids play… that’s not diversity. That’s disrespect.

And let’s be real — some newcomers don’t know the history. Don’t know this neighborhood lost half its factories in the ’90s. Don’t know we’ve been begging for better clinics, safer streets, for decades. Then suddenly, services show up — translators, outreach workers, housing aid — and it feels like *they* get more attention than folks born here. That breeds tension. Not because we hate them — but because we feel forgotten.

So yeah, more communication’s needed. Not lectures. Not slogans on a poster. Just… conversations. Like neighbors used to have on porches. “Hey, back home, what was it like?” “Here, we do it this way — mind telling me how you do it there?” That kind of thing.

Tolerance? Sure — I’ll tolerate a lot. But it works better when it’s mutual. When people aren’t just *putting up* with each other, but actually trying to *see* each other. That’s how you build something that holds.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character09_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness? Fairness is this: if you’ve been here your whole life, paying taxes outta every check — even when the work was rough, even when the boss didn’t care — then you *should* get first shot at a job. That’s how it used to be. That’s how it *ought* to be.

I remember working at that plastics plant before it closed. Ten years I put in — not because I loved it, but ’cause it paid the light bill and kept food in the fridge. When they started bringing in temporary workers — some with visas, some just here under the table — paying them less, giving them no benefits, I saw guys like me lose shifts. Not ’cause we were lazy. Not ’cause we weren’t showing up. But ’cause they could hire someone who wouldn’t complain, wouldn’t ask for safety gear, wouldn’t call OSHA when the fumes got bad.

That ain’t fair.

Now — don’t get me wrong. If there’s work nobody wants? Harvesting crops in 100-degree heat, cleaning hospital floors at midnight, working in meatpacking plants where people get hurt all the time — fine. Bring folks in to do those jobs. But *only* if locals had a real chance first. Post the job. Pay a decent wage. See who applies. If Americans won’t take it at that pay, then yeah — maybe bring in migrant labor. But don’t undercut us. Don’t use them as cheap replacements so companies can pocket the difference.

And here’s another thing — if you’re gonna bring people in, make sure they’re not draining the same broken system we’re stuck in. We’ve got schools with three kids sharing one textbook. ERs so backed up you wait twelve hours for stitches. Section 8 waiting lists ten years long. Now add more people — especially if they’re not paying into the system, not speaking English, needing translators, extra services — and it feels like the boat’s sinking while we’re still bailing water.

So balance? Here’s how I see it:  
- Jobs go to citizens and legal residents first. Period.  
- If there’s a real shortage — not just a company wanting cheaper labor — then bring in migrants on *temporary*, monitored programs. Tied to specific jobs, specific places. No open-ended promises.  
- And no welfare access for undocumented folks. Learn to stand on your own two feet, like the rest of us had to.

I know some say that’s harsh. But I’ve stood in food lines. I’ve had my power cut off in winter. Nobody flew in to help me. Nobody gave me a housing voucher or a free lawyer. So when I see newcomers getting support I never saw, it stings. Not because I want to keep it from them — but because I want the rules to be the same for everyone.

Fairness isn’t about keeping people out. It’s about making sure those of us already here — the ones who stayed through the layoffs, the decay, the neglect — aren’t punished for sticking around.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright. Let’s lay it out like I see it — not from some news clip or politician’s speech, but from what I’ve lived and seen with my own eyes.

First, yeah — immigrants *do* fill jobs a lot of Americans won’t take. Farm work. Janitorial. Some of the nastier factory lines. I’ll give ’em that. And I ain’t blind — places like the meatpacking plant in Iowa or the orchards out West? They’d shut down overnight if you suddenly deported half the crew. So on that point — labor shortages — there’s truth. But here’s what they don’t say: those jobs wouldn’t be short-staffed if they paid decent wages and treated people right. Pay someone $25 an hour to gut hogs in that heat, offer health care, safe conditions — you’d find American workers. The reason they can’t fill ’em? ‘Cause they’re exploiting cheap labor, plain and simple. So I respect the work, but I don’t respect how the system uses it.

Cultural diversity? Sure, adds flavor. I’ve eaten Ethiopian food, been to a Diwali festival once with a buddy — was different, but not bad. Music, food, clothes — that stuff’s fine. But when people talk about “vitality,” sometimes it sounds like they’re erasing us. Like our towns, our way of life, don’t matter. Like we’re supposed to just accept that everything changes while nobody asks us. And let’s be real — most of the folks pushing “diversity” live in safe neighborhoods, work office jobs, don’t have to deal with the fallout when things go sideways. They don’t see the overcrowded ERs or the schools where half the kids speak no English. So I’ll take the good parts of diversity, but don’t sell it like it’s all sunshine. Not when people feel pushed aside.

Security? Yeah, I think about it. Not every immigrant’s a threat — far from it. Most are just trying to survive, same as anyone. But I’ve seen small towns turn rough overnight after certain groups moved in — gangs, drugs, violence. And not all of it’s media hype. I knew a guy in Allentown whose sister got jumped outside her apartment by a group of guys who came in under refugee resettlement — one of ’em had a record back home they didn’t tell us about. She ended up in the hospital. That sticks with you.

I’m not saying close the borders. But I *am* saying: vet people properly. Check their background. Make sure they’re not bringing danger with them. And if someone’s here illegally and commits a crime? Kick ’em out. No second chances for that. We don’t let our own people off when they do wrong — why should we hand a free pass to someone who broke the law just to get here?

Humanitarian side? That cuts deep. I’ve seen pictures of kids in camps, families fleeing war zones. It hurts. If my kids were starving or getting shot at, I’d run too. So refugees — people truly running for their lives — yeah, we should help. But *in order*. Not bypassing legal lines while citizens wait years. Not dumping them in struggling towns without support, then acting surprised when tensions rise. Help them — but don’t make *us* pay the full price.

And the fear about jobs and wages? That’s not fear. That’s fact. I lived it. When companies bring in H-1B tech workers for less than local engineers, when farms hire undocumented crews at sub-minimum rates, when construction bosses use day laborers who don’t complain about broken ladders — wages go down for everyone. My cousin’s a welder. Used to make $24 an hour. Now he’s lucky to get $18 — ’cause there’s always some new guy willing to work cheaper, no questions asked. That’s not conspiracy — that’s what happens when supply outpaces demand.

So which views are reasonable?  
- Labor shortage argument? Reasonable — *if* the jobs are truly undesirable and fairly paid.  
- Humanitarian aid? Reasonable — *if* done legally, safely, and without ignoring those already here.  
- Security concerns? Reasonable — especially when screening is weak or ignored.  
- Cultural pride? Fine — but don’t act like tradition and belonging don’t matter to working people.

What needs more facts? Maybe the exact numbers — how many crimes are *actually* committed by undocumented vs. citizens, how much taxes they really pay, long-term impact on schools and hospitals. I’d listen to that. But don’t come at me with charts while I’m watching my neighborhood change faster than I can understand it. Data matters — but so does what we *feel*, what we *see* every day.

At the end of the day, I want honesty. Not slogans. Not guilt trips. Just straight talk: we can help others — but not by stepping on the backs of the people who built this country with calloused hands and busted knees.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for any one of those extremes — not complete openness, and sure as hell not shutting the door completely. That’s all theory, politics, TV talk. Out here in the real world, you need something that actually *works* — something fair to people already here, but doesn’t turn our backs on folks trying to do right.

If it were up to me? A mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, **with strict numerical limits**, and **tight enforcement of legal status**. And no — I don’t care how sad the story is — if you’re not in legally, you don’t get first dibs on anything.

Here’s how I’d see it:

First — **job-based entry**, but only when there’s a *proven* shortage. Not just “we want cheaper labor.” I mean: post the job locally, pay union-scale or above, wait 60 days. If no citizen or legal resident takes it — *then* bring in foreign workers. But tie their visa to that job, that location. No hopping around. When the job ends, they go home — unless they apply through the same line everyone else does. That keeps companies from gaming the system and underpaying immigrants while freezing out locals.

Second — **numerical limits**. Not zero. Not open season. A set number every year, based on what our schools, hospitals, and housing can actually handle. Not what some billionaire says is “good for growth,” but what regular towns like mine can absorb without breaking. Ten thousand? Fifty? I don’t know the exact number — but it should be firm, transparent, and adjusted only after looking at real strain on services. And yeah — prioritize people who speak English, have skills, family ties *already here legally*, or come from allied countries. Not because I hate anyone — but because integration goes smoother when people can communicate and contribute fast.

Third — **no tolerance for illegal entry**, especially for work. If you cross the border unlawfully, you don’t get amnesty. You don’t get benefits. You don’t stay. Get caught? Sent back. Fast. No years in court. No loopholes. Otherwise, why would anyone come the right way? My grandpa came from Ireland — took *years*, filled out papers, waited his turn. Why should someone sneak across today get treated better?

And while we’re at it — crack down on employers who hire undocumented workers. Fine ’em hard. Shut ’em down if they keep doing it. That’s the root of the problem — not the workers, but the bosses using them to cut costs. That’s what kills wages and breeds resentment.

Now — about refugees? Different category. But still — vet thoroughly. Health checks, background checks, no gang ties, no extremist links. Bring them in small numbers, place them where communities agree to take them — not dumped in struggling cities already stretched thin. And make sure aid comes with them — housing, language classes, job training — so they’re not just another burden on folks barely scraping by.

Fairness, to me, means this:  
- Follow the rules, earn your place — and you’re welcome.  
- Skip the line, break the law — and you lose your shot.  
- Need help fleeing danger? We’ll help — but not at the cost of our own stability.

Social integration happens when people learn English, respect local laws, and try to fit in — not when we’re expected to adapt to ten different languages and customs overnight while nobody lifts a finger to meet us halfway.

So yeah — job-based, limited, controlled, enforced. That’s the balance. Not perfect. But fair. And honest. That’s all I ever wanted — for things to be straight-up, not twisted for politicians or corporations. Let people come — but come right. Stay true — but don’t act like the country we knew doesn’t matter anymore.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character09_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character09_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did.

Sitting here, talking like him — not just *about* him, but *as* him — it brought something back I hadn’t felt in a while. Not just his opinions, but the weight behind them. The tiredness. The pride. The way he wasn’t trying to hate anybody, but just kept getting made to feel invisible.

I’ll admit — when he was alive, sometimes I thought he was too hard on things. Too stuck on “this is how we do it here” or suspicious of change. I used to chalk it up to where he came from — limited schooling, small town, never traveled much. Thought maybe he just didn’t get it.

But doing this today… I see now it wasn’t ignorance. It was fear. Not of people, really — but of being erased. Of working your whole life, playing by the rules, and then watching others get chances you never had, while nobody even sees *you* as someone worth helping.

He wasn’t against immigrants. He was against the system that used them to undercut guys like him — then blamed *him* for being angry about it. He wanted fairness to mean something real, not just a word tossed around by people who never punched a time clock.

And honestly? This made me rethink my own stance. I’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming — which I still believe in. But I used to think concerns about jobs, crime, culture — those were overblown. Just fear-mongering. Now I see: they’re rooted in real experience. You can’t dismiss a man’s pain just because it doesn’t fit a progressive narrative.

That doesn’t mean I agree with every boundary he’d draw. Maybe I’d allow a bit more flexibility, a longer runway for integration. But I get it now — belonging has to go both ways. You can’t demand loyalty to a community if you never let that community speak.

So yeah… I feel closer to him today than I have in years. Not because I’ve become him — but because I finally *heard* him. Not as a stereotype — “angry White working-class guy” — but as a person who loved this place, feared losing it, and just wanted to matter.

And maybe… that’s the lesson. Policy shouldn’t be built on guilt or anger — but on listening. To him. To newcomers. To everyone in between. Because if we don’t make space for voices like his, we don’t build unity — we just build silence. And silence breaks communities faster than any border ever could.
